<reason>B more convincingly isolates the choice between predictable assistance and a protected allocation. Its procurement alternative preserves substantial planning benefits without requiring Ukraine's standing floor, while its pressure questions expose A's unusually restrictive suspension threshold. A establishes plausible deterrence benefits but never adequately weighs them against preventive defense elsewhere. Its closing also misreads B's acknowledgment of uncertainty as conceding that reallocation and retreat are indistinguishable, despite B identifying observable reinforcements that distinguish them.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B directly answers A's product-mix defense: contracts can specify weapons and quantities without permanently guaranteeing their destination. It then turns A's existential-threat threshold against A's deterrence case: competing defenses may deserve reinforcement before danger becomes existential.</best_rebuttal>
